Finance Minister Nhlanhla Nene

By: Este de Klerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
How will newly appointed Finance Minister Nene steer the economy that is heading in the direction of another recession, how will he improve business relations and international investor confidence?

Summary:
How will newly appointed Finance Minister Nene steer the economy that is heading in the direction of another recession, how will he improve business relations and international investor confidence?

South Africa is Africa's most advanced economy, but can we remain the prime investment destination?
Minister Nhlanhla Nene said that an uneven demand from aborad and the protracted mining strike capped South Africa's economic growth at around 2% this year. That could stoke continued volatility in the value of the country's currency, the rand and interrupt plans to narrow the budget deficit and it would be a challenge to achieve the numbers government had penciled in.

How will he guide through this and what other plans will he put in place?
Who is he and why will he make a good Minister of Finance?
What does the future hold for the South African economy in his view?

Script:


MINISTER OF FINANCE

PRODUCER: ESTé DE KLERK

JOHN VO: The financial crisis of 2009 took the world to the economic brink. Five years later, there are signs of a recovery.

JOHN LINK: Compared to many countries around the world - including Spain, Greece and Ireland - South Africa navigated its way through the global financial meltdown quite successfully. Despite massive job losses, our government was generally praised for its response to the crisis. Fast forward to 2014, and it seems our economy might well be shrinking once again. Our new Finance Minister, Nhlanhla Nene, has a tough job on his hands.

[PLATINUM STRIKE VISUALS]

MINISTER NHLANHLA NENE/MINISTER OF FINANCE: We started the year with the mining strike, that unrest actually ran through for five months, close to six months. That had an impact on our economy which was not growing that fast even at that point.

JOHN VO: Nene has had no time to ease into his new position, as South Africa lurches from one labour dispute to the next. The recent Platinum Belt strike wasn’t only one of the country’s longest ever, but also one of its costliest: in February, the Chamber of Mines estimated the country was hemorrhaging up to R400 million a day. The country rejoiced when a deal was signed, but that’s when the metal workers downed tools. Manufacturing and mining account for a fifth of the South African economy.

JOHN: What are the major differences between 2008/2009, the global financial crisis and the period of uncertainty we are going through now?

MINISTER NENE: Look, in 2009, you would recall, we had built fiscal space that had allowed us time. So, now we have a situation where we were just recovering from that. The new challenges that kicked in now, most of them are actually within our borders, but it is now coupled with our vulnerability to the external shocks as well.

John Link: So, our economy is under siege on two fronts and some have questioned whether Nene is the right person to organise our defences. But, while he may lack the profile of Pravin Gordhan, the man he succeeded, and the flamboyance of Trevor Manuel, the country’s longest serving Finance Minister, he acted as deputy to both. And the business community is hoping their approach to managing the country’s finances rubbed off on him.

JOHN: Do you think that your job is more difficult that your immediate predecessors?

MINISTER NENE: You know, each term has its own challenges. When Minister Gordon came into office, we shared some of the burden. It gave me an understanding of the environment in which we operate.

JOHN VO: Unlike some of his former principals in the Finance Ministry, Nene is wary of the limelight. Nor is he known for the colourful soundbites that characterised Manuel’s time in office.

TREVOR MANUEL: We will ride out this storm together on a strength and the vision and a plan of action that we can be proud of as South Africans.

JOHN VO: Even a question about Nene’s appointment draws a measured response.

JOHN: Did you ever imagine that you would get here, Minister, that you would be top of the pile, that you would be deciding the direction this country take?

MINISTER NENE: Not exactly, I have been given an opportunity in the past, from local government, went into Parliament. One is actually part of a team that has worked tirelessly to get the country to where it is.

John Link: If there’s a word you hear from Minister Nene more often than others, that word is teamwork. Managing the country’s finances requires a close working relationship with Reserve Bank Governor, Gill Marcus. It fell to her to announce earlier this month that interest rates were going up, and that the bank had changed its outlook on economic growth. It was down from a low 2.8% to an even lower 1.7%.

JOHN: Both you and the Reserve Bank Governor, Gill Marcus have been more optimistic about the country’s economy, so, are we in recession or not?

MINISTER NENE: We are not in recession yet, and we are working very hard not to get there. We actually want the economy to grow. Whilst we want to get the economy to full employment, whilst we want price stability, but all that happens within an environment of an economy that should be growing and if it is growing we are in a better position to deal with the other indicators.

JOHN VO: When mining production dropped by 24,7% in the first three months of the year, not all areas looked so bleak. Agriculture grew by 2,5% and construction by 4,5%.

MINISTER NENE: If you look at that and you aggregate that, you realize that there are some areas that if we focus on, there are areas of growth, so the potential for actually turning things around is there and if we implement what is on the table, the prospects for economic development and growth are at hand.

John Link: The government is pinning the country’s economic prospects on the National Development Plan. It’s a wide ranging roadmap that guides the country’s development between now and 2030. It was adopted by Parliament in 2012, but its reception in some quarters, including from inside Cabinet, has been lukewarm. Its implementation now seems non-negotiable.

VO: The NDP is nothing if not ambitious. It promises 11-million jobs, as well as clean water, electricity, sanitation, quality education and safe and reliable public transport for all South Africans. In February, President Zuma told Parliament implementing the plan will be government’s main focus during the next five years, and it’ll fall to Nene to ensure there’s enough cash available to meet those objectives.

JOHN: What will the National Development Plan mean for the average man and woman in the street?

MINISTER NENE: The National Development Plan is built on a number of pillars, but key among those is reducing the cost of doing business and also reducing the cost of living for the poor and that is done in a number of ways, removing red-tape and making sure that you have an environment that is conducive to doing business.

JOHN VO: Having a roadmap is one thing, implementing it is quite another. And, when it comes to taking advantage of the current investment bonanza in many parts of Africa, some critics say our current policies have let us down. Proof, they say, lies in April’s announcement that Nigeria had overtaken us as Africa’s biggest economy.

JOHN: Countries like Mozambique growing very fast, Tanzania, Rwanda, are they better at managing their economies than we have been?

MINISTER NENE: I don’t think it is also just about a comparison between ourselves and those economies, it is actually about doing better where we are because performance should actually be measured by our growth in relation to our previous performance, but at the same time, if you identify areas of growth in Africa, we should also be looking at an opportunity of increasing our trade.

JOHN VO: But, improving on our past performance isn’t easy when credit rating agencies like Standard and Poor’s have gradually decreased our credit rating over the past few years – which means it costs more for us to borrow money from international institutions.

John Link: And if our country’s finances are looking a little unhealthy, then it’s inevitable that we too will start feeling the economic pinch. And when that happens, the complexities of the global financial system and the impact of ratings agencies are furthest from mind.

JOHN: The average South African, Minister, is not necessarily a businessperson, doesn’t necessarily have a business background. What they know is how much something costs, how much buying a house costs in interest and so forth. What is your message to them?

MINISTER NENE: The message is we need to live within our means, but we also all need to work very hard. We also should take advantage of the opportunities that are presented by the new dispensation to create opportunities for ourselves and take advantage of them.
